title: Same seven keys, different tree
hook: A search tree halves the work at every step. Unless you fill it in the wrong order.

knows: binary search halves a sorted list (binary-search)
doesNotKnow: how a binary search tree is built by inserting keys one at a time
that the tree's shape, and so its depth, depends on the insertion order

misconception: A binary search tree is always shallow, so a lookup always takes about log2 n steps.
objective: The learner can explain that inserting keys in sorted order makes a binary search tree a chain (7 keys, 7 levels), while a mixed order such as 4 2 6 1 3 5 7 gives 3 levels, so the tree's speed depends on insertion order.

claims.text: Inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in that order into an empty binary search tree makes a chain 7 levels deep.
claims.source: Demo.tsx build(): standard BST insertion (smaller left, larger or equal right). Builder ran it in Node: levels([1..7]) = 7. Each key exceeds all earlier keys so it becomes the right child of the previous key.

claims.text: Inserting the same keys in the order 4 2 6 1 3 5 7 gives a tree 3 levels deep, so any key is at most 3 steps from the top.
claims.source: Demo.tsx build(): levels([4,2,6,1,3,5,7]) = 3 (builder ran in Node). A complete tree of 2^3 - 1 = 7 nodes has 3 levels. · Fact-check 2026-10-13: Depth 3 counts nodes on the path; the reveal uses "steps" the same way for both trees (3 vs 7), consistent.

claims.text: In a binary search tree each new key walks down from the top, going left if smaller and right if larger, until it finds an empty spot.
Sorted input turns a binary search tree into a list: n keys give n levels.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., 12.1 and 12.4: tree height ranges from about lg n to n - 1 edges (n levels); inserting keys in increasing order yields a chain.

claims.text: Libraries use self-balancing trees to keep the tree shallow whatever the insertion order.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., ch. 13 (red-black trees, height at most 2 lg(n+1)); Java's TreeMap and C++ std::map are documented/implemented as red-black trees (OpenJDK TreeMap javadoc: 'A Red-Black tree based NavigableMap implementation').

recall.question: A program stores 1,000 usernames in a plain binary search tree, adding them in alphabetical order. How many steps can a lookup take in the worst case?
options: About 10, because a tree halves the search
About 1,000, because the tree is a chain
recall.why: Alphabetical order is sorted input: each name is larger than all before it, so each hangs to the right of the last and the tree becomes a 1,000-level chain.
